result: Repaired survey filed at docs/design/16-early-unlocks-survey.md on origin/main (note commit 6986e12, writing verdict commit d8d52fb). The note compares all seven requested delivery patterns by lesson and relative build cost, and gives substantive farming/life-sim, survival-crafting, colony-sim, roguelike, Metroidvania, and tower-defence comparisons. The colony section separates deterministic research/proof from event arrivals; the other repaired sections explain what transfers to Tiny Farm and what would need to be built. Named external mechanics link to developer/publisher sources where possible. It ranks owned-material reuse, visible milestone proof, and visible restoration provisionally for this game. Current harvest-to-replant and bin reserve are already implemented under S-18 to S-20; a playable silo and its acquisition rule are not. This is research, not implementation of a silo, pea ammo, or robot unlocks. Both source card fields remain truncated at “Note that if w” and “given: the player may not be able to read ”; their missing endings are unknown, so the exact final ranking and silo acquisition remain provisional. The prior result and checker concerns are retained. Focused note-coverage assertions, git diff --check, and tools/check_writing.py --verify passed; the report skill’s optional scripts/check_report.py is absent from this repository. GitHub Actions run 35977925899 for d8d52fb passed writing, gateway, and Godot tests. This closure is an interactive operator review of the repaired brief, not a new native HQ checker verdict or Daniel acceptance.

recommend.answer: Provisional candidate: a visible production proof followed by repairing a silo already visible on the land. No acquisition rule is settled by this survey.

recommend.instead: A timed shipment or neighbour gift could present an unlock, but needs a guaranteed route and additional wordless teaching.

prior_results.result:
Survey done — nothing in the repo changed, this was a reading task.

**How other games hand a player something new without money changing hands, and what each costs to build:**

- **A gift that arrives on a timer** (Stardew Valley's mail, Animal Crossing's mailbox). Teaches: come back tomorrow, the world moves without you. Cheap once a day-turn already exists, but it reads as luck rather than something earned.
- **A neighbour who gives you something for doing a favor** (Stardew's community bundles, village requests in Harvest Moon/Animal Crossing). Teaches: helping someone pays you back. Needs a request/quest tracker and, without any on-screen text, a whole vocabulary of icons to ask for and confirm the favor — the heaviest of these seven to build wordlessly.
- **A tool sitting in the world, found rather than bought** (chests in Zelda, seeds in Stardew's mines). Teaches: exploring pays off. Cheap if picking it up reuses a verb the player already has.
- **A milestone unlock** — the game notices you've proven something and opens the next thing (Terraria's boss drops, Slay the Spire's relics). Teaches: mastery is rewarded, and it reads without a word if the celebration is visual. Cheap when the game already tracks the state that proves it.
- **Crafting from what you already have** — the things you gather combine into the next thing (Don't Starve, Terraria's workbench). Teaches: what you're holding has more than one use. Wordless by nature — an icon of the ingredient next to an icon of the result says the whole rule.
- **Fixing something broken that was already on your land** (Stardew's derelict farm and community center, My Time at Portia's ruins). Teaches: the land itself tells you what's coming, not a shop. No economy needed at all — the cost is materials and effort, not gold.
- **A seasonal or weather windfall** — something only shows up on certain days (Stardew's traveling cart, Animal Crossing's shooting stars). Teaches: pay attention to the calendar. Needs a calendar-driven spawn table, and this game doesn't have seasons yet, so it's weaker ground to build on right now.

Roguelikes and Metroidvanias mostly recombine these rather than invent new ones: a roguelike's "pick one of three" level-up is the milestone pattern with a choice attached; a Metroidvania's ability-behind-a-boss fuses milestone-unlock with found-in-world. Tower defense's usual free unlock — clear this wave, open the next tower — is the milestone pattern again.

**Top three for this game, ranked:**

1. **Crafting from what you already have** — this is what you described: a harvested plant becomes next season's seed, or becomes a consumable like the pea for a pea-shooter. Cheapest to build (it reuses the pouch and action system that already exist) and the most wordless of all seven — watching a crop turn back into a seed teaches the rule by itself.
2. **Milestone unlock**, for the storage upgrades. The game already runs on this pattern everywhere else, so extending it to "excess" thresholds (5 or 10 on your person, more with a grain silo) costs almost nothing new to build or to teach.
3. **Repair/restore**, for the grain silo itself. Rather than buying it from the shop — which puts storage right back behind money, the thing this change is trying to remove — she finds it broken down on the land and fixes it. Wordless, and matches the yard-clearing already in the game.

I'd hold off on the neighbour-favor and timed-gift patterns for now — not wrong, just heavier to build wordlessly, and better suited once the game has more icon vocabulary to draw on.

**Two things worth knowing:**
- The pea-shooter isn't a new idea — a "pea economy" is already queued for the defense-system pass: peas ship now as an ordinary crop, and a shooter/tower that consumes them is designed later. Your seed-rework and that queued item are the same design; whoever writes the strawman should write them together.
- Your note reached me cut off twice — once mid-sentence ("Note that if w—") and once in the constraints you gave for the ranking ("given: the player may not be able to read—"). I ranked against the one constraint I already know holds for this part of the game (no reading required), but I didn't guess at what either cut-off sentence was going to say. Worth resending if there was more there.
